extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in political economy, public choice, and regulatory policy; policy analysts studying agency oversight and interest-group monitoring
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical principal-agent model analyzing interest-group (IG) monitoring of regulatory agencies: how IGs report signals, principals' payments, collusion risks, and when IG-monitoring is more efficient than 'uninterested' monitoring. Derives equilibrium comparative statics, propositions, and numerical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption 1: Increasing hazard rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The hazard rate w'(e)/(1-w(e)) increases with effort e; formally -w''(e)(1-w(e)) < w'(e)^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard information-economics assumption implies that, conditional on a low outcome not having occurred, increasing effort makes a high outcome each time more likely. It is satisfied by many densities (e.g., n(e)=θ(2-e^{-1}) for θ in (1/2,1)). Used to guarantee second-order conditions and uniqueness of interior solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption 2: Bounded curvature of density
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio -w''(e)/w'(e) decreases with e but not too fast; specifically an inequality (given in text) must hold so the first-order approach remains valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical condition (about second derivatives) together with Assumption 1 supports the validity of replacing continuum incentive constraints with first-order conditions (see Rogerson 1985) and ensures maxima satisfy second-order conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-order approach and IRCA non-binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first-order (local) approach to replace the continuum of incentive constraints by w_j(e_j)[V(T_j)-V(T_p)] = 1; assume the agent's individual rationality constraint (IRCA) is not binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifies analysis: continuum of ICs becomes a first-order condition; interior solution requires T_high > T_low. The authors note conditions that make this approach valid and assume IRCA is not binding throughout sections deriving equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegativity of transfers / transfer normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfers must be nonnegative; given C wants high outcomes and P wants low outcomes, certain transfers are zero in equilibrium (e.g., T_p = 0 in some cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption simplifies algebra and yields corner solutions in some setups. It also underlies conclusions about who must satisfy IRCA alone (e.g., C) and the shape of equilibrium payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor participation cost c_M and its role
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost to the monitor of obtaining/participating (c_M) can be zero (monitor participates) or positive (monitor may not be worthwhile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When c_M = 0 monitoring is economically available and IGs may serve as ex-ante monitors; when c_M > 0 participation must be subsidized and duplication of monitoring costs matters (principals will not subsidize more than two opposed IGs in single-dimensional framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex-post vs ex-ante monitoring efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest-group monitors are not more efficient than 'regular' (uninterested) monitors at ex-post monitoring, but may be more efficient at ex-ante monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the monitor's information is ex-post (about realized effort), the monitor's preferences over outcomes are irrelevant and any compensated monitor will report; for ex-ante information (about shocks prior to agent action), interest groups can improve information provision and reduce agents' informational rents relative to ex-post-only monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor reporting incentives absent payments (fire-alarm behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: If left unpaid, an interested monitor optimally discloses only low-productivity (bad) shocks and withholds high-productivity (good) shocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reporting high-productivity signals reduces the net incentive transfer and thus may not be in the IG's interest, IGs mimic 'fire-alarm' strategies: report when revelation makes principals (and group) better off, withhold otherwise. This replicates McCubbins & Schwartz (1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for principals to buy a high-productivity report
rubrics_metrics.description: A signal s(θ)=f_h(θ) will be released only if the sum of rewards offered by C and P exceeds the monitor's expected utility loss from reporting: S_c(f_h)+S_p(f_h) > m[ ... positive bracketed term ... ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right-hand-side is the monitor's expected loss (money equivalent) from revealing a high-productivity shock; principals must collectively compensate at least that amount. This yields explicit willingness-to-pay thresholds and potential free-rider problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-rider / coordination failure among principals
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when joint acquisition of a monitor's signal is profitable, coordination failure (private incentives) can leave principals uninformed because each hopes the other will pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The game can result in Nash equilibria where no principal pays for a valuable report; numerical example shows thresholds of m under which C or P alone or both can buy the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collusion between agent and monitor — feasibility and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Collusion (agent bribing monitor to withhold or reveal signals) is possible; preventing collusion requires paying the monitor at least the combined loss the monitor and/or agent would suffer from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the monitor is interested and suffers disutility from collusion, collusion is harder and more costly for the agent; if monitor is uninterested, preventing collusion requires paying the monitor the agent's direct utility loss. Thus, IG-monitors can make collusion-proof contracting cheaper depending on preferences and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple interest-group monitors with opposed preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple IG-monitors with opposed preferences participate, principals obtain essentially the same information as with an uninterested monitor, and the cost of preventing collusion is lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With opposed IGs, at least one monitor will want to freely release each type of signal; if monitoring costs are zero, multiple opposed IGs are more efficient than a single uninterested monitor. If c_M > 0, relative efficiency depends on IG gains from participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1: Productivity shocks and implemented effort
rubrics_metrics.description: When marginal productivity of effort is lower (higher) than expected, the implemented level of effort when two principals are equally uninformed results in a lower (higher) effort than the expected level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: principals set transfers based on expected marginal cost of inducing effort; misestimation of productivity leads to over- or under-payment and thus implemented effort deviates from expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2: Effect of increased productivity on transfers and effort
rubrics_metrics.description: If C and P are informed of u (productivity), and if π(e) > 1/2 or π(e) = α(2-e^{-1}), then exogenously increasing u will reduce the net incentive transfer (T_C - T_P) and increase the agent's equilibrium effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, greater expected productivity can both lower net payments and raise effort; this drives the monitor's incentive to withhold good-news signals absent payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2: Monitor's disclosure rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When the IG-monitor observes f_L(θ) it discloses the information; when it observes f_h(θ) it prefers to hide it absent positive payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the IG 'fire-alarm' tendency: IGs will only alert principals about states that make principals (and the IG) better off, and demand payoffs to reveal states that reduce their utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent's signaling incentives with single vs multiple principals
rubrics_metrics.description: With a single principal who wants high outcomes, the agent prefers to be perceived as less efficient (low productivity). With multiple principals, the sign of the agent's incentive to misreport can change; under certain π(e) forms (e.g., π(e)=α(2-e^{-1})), the agent prefers to be seen as highly productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects whether the agent will bribe a monitor to withhold bad signals or to reveal good ones; incentive-compatibility requires compensating monitors accordingly to make contracts collusion-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma/Proposition on collusion costs and efficiency (Lemma 3 & Proposition 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple IG-monitors with opposed preferences participate, principals' information, expected outcome, and effort equal those under an uninterested monitor, while the cost of preventing collusion is lower when IG-monitors are used. If c_M = 0, multiple opposed IGs are more efficient than uninterested monitors; if c_M > 0, relative efficiency depends on IG gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: allow multiple IG participation (as APA sec.6(a) does) to replicate benefits of an uninterested monitor at lower collusion-prevention cost, but weigh monitoring cost subsidies if c_M>0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principals' payment thresholds and numerical example guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Principals' maximum willingness to pay for a report equals the increase in their expected utilities (ΔEUC, ΔEUP); the monitor's marginal utility m determines who can profitably buy the report (numerical thresholds given in example: C pays up to 0.004022, P up to 0.01579; joint feasible if m below specified thresholds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computed ΔEU and m to determine whether C alone, P alone, or both jointly will purchase a report; inability to coordinate can lead to lost opportunities even when acquisition is jointly profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principals will not subsidize more than two opposed IGs (single-dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the single-dimensional framework, principals will not subsidize participation of more than two IG-monitors with opposed interests because two suffice to obtain all information monitors can produce; additional IGs duplicate monitoring costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation rule: each IG's gain from participation must at least cover half its monitoring cost for principals' total subsidy to be lower than the cost of a single uninterested monitor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex-post monitoring compensation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the monitor's information is about realized effort (ex-post), the monitor's preferences about outcomes are irrelevant; the monitor will report any signal received provided a compensation is offered, and that compensation is a function of the agency's potential loss from release rather than the monitor's preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus for ex-post monitoring, IGs are neither more nor less efficient in principle, because payment can be set equal to agency loss; IG advantage arises mainly for ex-ante information provision.
